Buster Keaton. Born Joseph Frank Keaton in 1895, an American actor, filmmaker, and acrobat who perfected the stone-faced style of physical comedy in silent film. Rivaling Charlie Chaplin as the era's greatest comedian, Keaton's films are celebrated for their mathematical precision, innovative camera work, and breathtaking stunts—all performed with an inscrutable facial expression that became his trademark. Where Chaplin wrung tears from laughter, Keaton wrung wonder from geometric impossibility. His cinema is architecture, not emotion.

Keaton's signature deadpan expression—an immobile, sorrowful face maintained even during extreme physical comedy—became iconic. He rarely smiled or broke character, trusting the gag itself to register the humor. His restraint created a unique effect. The audience laughs at the situation, not with the character, making viewers co-conspirators in recognizing absurdity that the character does not. Unlike Chaplin's sentimental vulnerability, Keaton's protagonists are rational men encountering irrational circumstances, their confusion and resolve generating comedy from logic colliding with chaos.

The General from 1926 is regarded as one of the finest comedies ever made. Keaton plays a railroad engineer in the Civil War pursuing a stolen locomotive, blending slapstick with genuine suspense and narrative logic. The gags are the plot. Sherlock Jr., made in 1924, features Keaton as a film projectionist who dreams himself into a movie and engages in surreal, impossible interactions with the film itself—an early story within a story that anticipated modernist cinema and influenced later experimental filmmakers. Our Hospitality from 1923 integrates location cinematography filmed on the Truckee River in natural settings with narrative coherence, pioneering the use of landscape for both visual beauty and comedic effect.

Keaton performed virtually all his own dangerous stunts. In Steamboat Bill, Jr. from 1928, a two-ton building facade fell around him—he passed through a window opening—a near-death moment that became cinema legend. The Playhouse from 1921 exploited split-screen and matte photography so Keaton appeared to play an entire theater full of performers, technical innovation serving comedy. Keaton was a mathematician of gags. His films are structured like geometric proofs, each scene building logically from the previous, creating a sense of inevitability rather than surprise.

His career arc mirrors the changing valuation of different kinds of cinema. Triumphant in the 1920s, nearly destroyed by the transition to sound when he was initially given bad scripts and directors, then rediscovered by cinephiles and scholars in the 1950s through 1970s. His work was dismissed for decades as mere slapstick until critics recognized the engineering precision underlying his gags and the philosophical weight of his narratives. His influence extended to modernist and avant-garde cinema. Filmmakers from Sergei Eisenstein to Jacques Tati studied Keaton's structural logic and visual precision. His refusal to sentimentalize or appeal directly to the audience now reads as almost austere in its discipline—the opposite of everything post-sound cinema would come to value. Yet precisely that rigor has allowed his films to outlast Chaplin's in some respects. Chaplin's emotional appeals can seem dated, but Keaton's structures feel timeless.
